title: Through-seawater links beyond the acoustic range–rate ceiling

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a sustained wireless connection through seawater that gives moving underwater vehicles substantially greater useful throughput over kilometres to tens of kilometres. It would carry supervisory commands and scientific sensor data while operating under specified coastal-water clarity, vehicle motion and sea conditions. Its defining achievement would combine range, delivered data rate, availability and practical deployment independence.

Existing transmission methods occupy different operating regimes. Acoustic absorption increases with frequency, constraining the bandwidth available over long distances. Blue–green optical transmission offers high rates over shorter distances that depend strongly on water clarity. Li, Chitre and Stojanovic give an approximate optical range of 100 m and a radio-frequency example of a few metres at about 10 kHz. These examples describe particular propagation conditions. Longer optical paths appear in the supplied experimental literature, including Zhang and colleagues’ secondary account of a 5 Mbps, 200 m deep-clear-water sea trial near Bermuda in April 2008.

Proposed scope. The service could connect a mobile pair directly or connect a vehicle through sparse relays without a dedicated support ship on scene. Shortening relay hops can increase available bandwidth, while adding infrastructure and making end-to-end performance depend on the complete route. A cable terminating at a fixed node supplies a connection point whose wireless reach to a free vehicle still requires demonstration.

significance.text: Acoustic communication already supports submerged sensor data collection, underwater robot control and coordination of autonomous vehicles. A substantial improvement in sustained mobile throughput and availability over tens of kilometres would expand those capabilities, allowing more frequent scientific data return and richer supervisory command with less dependence on nearby communication infrastructure. The revolutionary case rests on the size and operational durability of that improvement.

Li, Chitre and Stojanovic describe representative acoustic operation at a few kilobits per second over 10 km and illustrate the bandwidth constraint with about 1 kHz available to a single 100 km hop. Their comparison with difficult mobile-radio channels and satellite-like delays captures two separate problems, severe signal distortion and long propagation time. Greater throughput would improve data delivery, while responsive remote manipulation would additionally require suitable latency, reliability and control systems. Basin-scale video would require substantially greater throughput than the proposed minimum supervisory stream.

Benchmark interpretation. The historical target supplied with this concept, reliable 1 Mbps over at least 10 km without repeaters, represents a stronger throughput ambition. Its range–rate product is 10,000 km·kb/s. An approximately hundredfold comparison follows arithmetically if the research notes’ attributed 100 km·kb/s survey envelope is used as the denominator. That denominator remains unverified in the supplied evidence, and the 2024 review already reports an acoustic example reaching 270 km·kb/s. The magnitude of a breakthrough therefore needs an explicit, operationally comparable baseline.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability sought by this proposal is sustained, substantially improved useful throughput across operational distances while the communicating platforms move through realistic seawater conditions. Acoustic implementations must contend with frequency-dependent absorption, restricted bandwidth, mobile-channel distortion and long propagation delays. The supplied sources establish these engineering challenges. They leave the complete capability’s demonstration status through November 2026 unresolved.

Optical approaches must extend performance through attenuation and scattering while maintaining a usable optical path as platforms move. The fixed deep-sea experiment demonstrates substantial local throughput, and the folded swimming-pool experiment demonstrates signal recovery over a longer controlled optical path. Extending these achievements to kilometres of coastal seawater requires evidence of adequate received signal, alignment or acquisition capability, real-time processing and resilience to changing water and motion conditions.

Engineering synthesis. A complete service must also sustain its power budget, reconnect after interruptions and preserve delivered throughput across any relay route. Sparse infrastructure creates concrete design questions about relay spacing, station keeping, maintenance and availability. These system requirements need to be demonstrated alongside the physical channel improvement, with single-hop performance and end-to-end service measured separately.

current_state.text: The 2024 review by Li, Chitre and Stojanovic, published in Nature Reviews Electrical Engineering with DOI 10.1038/s44287-024-00122-w, documents the range–bandwidth tradeoff and the bandwidth advantage of shorter relay hops. It also reports Kida and colleagues’ acoustic transmission at up to 20 kbps over 13.5 km, with more than 98% of frames bit error-free. That example gives a range–rate product of 270 km·kb/s and overlaps a proposed starting threshold of tens of kilobits per second at 10 km. The supplied passage does not establish compliance with the full mobile, coastal-water, multiday service proposed here.

The research notes attribute several numerical summaries to Fewell, von Trojan and Steed’s March 2020 DSTG-GD-1101 survey. They describe an approximate acoustic at-sea envelope of 100 km·kb/s across ranges from about 1 km to thousands of kilometres, optical performance near 1000 m·Mb/s over roughly 5–200 m, lower radio range–rate products, and an approximately 2.5-fold acoustic improvement over twenty years. No text of that report was retained in the supplied source record, leaving these figures and their exact definitions unverified. An empirical survey envelope also requires interpretation in its original measurement context before it can support claims about a physical limit or subsequent progress.

Zhang and colleagues’ arXiv record, 2310.07718, gives submission on 23 July 2023 and revision on 13 December 2023, with related DOI 10.1109/MCOM.001.2300461. The supplied review includes both landing-page metadata and full-paper evidence. The paper reports a fixed optical deployment spanning 30 m at 1650 m depth, using a 125 Mbps green physical link and a 6.25 Mbps blue non-line-of-sight return link. Effective Ethernet bandwidths were 97.4 Mbps and 5.5 Mbps respectively, providing a more operational measure than physical bitrate alone.

The Zhang deployment’s error monitoring ran continuously for one hour each day over 30 days. Reported pre-forward-error-correction bit-error ratios were below 10^-5 for the green link and 10^-7 for the blue link. This establishes repeated sampled performance during a month-long deployment, with continuous multiday availability remaining outside the reported monitoring scope. The paper estimates maximum ranges of 117.7 m and 128.3 m when geometric loss is included, and 231.6 m and 337.5 m when it is omitted. Those calculations use deep-sea water-sample measurements and remain projected ranges.

Dong and colleagues’ retained arXiv manuscript, 2411.10674, reports 1 Gbps over a roughly 250 m folded optical path at a bit-error ratio of 3.4×10^-3. Four mirrors extended the path within a 50 m swimming pool. Synchronization, equalization and bit-error computation used offline MATLAB processing. The reported result establishes controlled-path experimental performance, with mobile real-time ocean operation requiring additional demonstration. The research notes assign a submission date of 16 November 2024 and journal DOI 10.1364/OE.549337, but the retained manuscript does not internally verify that metadata. An attempted journal full-text URL returned page-not-found, leaving journal pagination unverified.

Evidence boundary. The retained optical demonstrations establish high-rate short-range capabilities under their stated conditions. Their demonstrated scope falls short of the proposed 10 km and 50 km mobile service. The supplied record contains no freshness-search results establishing the complete frontier through 1 November 2026, so it cannot settle whether another system has achieved that service or how the acoustic frontier evolved after the cited work. The unavailable survey text and incomplete publication metadata limit interpretation without disproving the reported experiments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed operational demonstration. A mobile pair, or a vehicle communicating through explicitly bounded sparse relays without a dedicated support ship on scene, would carry a continuous supervisory and sensor stream over at least 10 km in coastal seawater, plus a lower but useful stream over at least 50 km, for multiple days. Before testing, the protocol should specify minimum net application rates at both distances, permissible relay count and spacing, whether the distances describe individual hops or the end-to-end route, and acceptable latency, outage and error performance. These are proposed criteria whose numerical details remain to be agreed.
completion_criteria.label: Sustain mobile 10 km and 50 km streams for days

completion_criteria.text: The 10 km starting target needs comparison with the reported acoustic result of up to 20 kbps over 13.5 km. Tens of kilobits per second at 10 km gains its significance from demonstrably improved sustained mobility, availability, environmental tolerance or infrastructure requirements, together with any throughput increase. A reliable 1 Mbps, 10 km repeater-free link would meet the stronger throughput benchmark. Meeting the complete operational proposal would additionally require its specified endurance, coastal-water, mobility and 50 km demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate gains against the 20 kbps, 13.5 km acoustic benchmark

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement and reproducibility requirements. Publish physical bitrate, net delivered throughput, pre- and post-correction error metrics, latency distributions, outages, reconnection times, power consumption and total operating duration. Report vehicle motion, depth, water clarity or turbidity, relevant sea conditions, geometry and relay topology. Continuous service logs should establish endurance, and repeated trials across independently characterized sites or seasons should establish demonstrated operating breadth. Independent replication or sufficiently complete hardware and processing descriptions would strengthen reproducibility.
completion_criteria.label: Report link performance and endurance across independently characterized operating conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary. A convincing claim should identify the tested environmental envelope and the conditions under which service degrades or fails. Tank and pool experiments, fixed links spanning tens of metres and isolated peak acoustic records remain valuable component evidence, while the complete claim requires an integrated operational trial. Finite tests would establish performance across the tested conditions, with broader seawater applicability remaining a question for further demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Integrated trials establish environmental operating limits and service failure conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. MNE-05, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing, shares potential signaling and infrastructure with this concept. Positioning can use low-rate exchanges, and its success depends on localization accuracy and availability. MNE-06 concerns delivered communication service over distance. MNE-10, Coherent observability of the deep-ocean volume, could use improved links to return and coordinate measurements, while still requiring its own sensing, coverage and data-integration capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis. MNE-07, Persistent abyssal work, with depth no longer the cost driver, could benefit from remote supervision and scientific data return at depth. MNE-08, Work-class underwater vehicles powered by the ocean, could pair sustained energy supply with communication-enabled operations. Their respective depth-cost and energy breakthroughs remain separate from the communication advance, although link power consumption and deployment support would affect practical integration.

Roster-based synthesis. MNE-01, Ship-scale collapse of turbulent skin friction, MNE-02, Merchant ships freed from the displacement-hull speed barrier, MNE-03, Seawater magnetohydrodynamic propulsion at propeller-class efficiency, and MNE-04, Controlled, sustained supercavitating travel, concern hydrodynamic or propulsion capabilities. Improved through-seawater links could support telemetry and supervision of relevant submerged platforms. Motion and platform geometry would also become operating conditions for communication trials. Each propulsion or drag-reduction entry retains its own performance requirements.

Roster-based synthesis. MNE-09, Storm-stable floating land in the open ocean, could provide surface infrastructure for underwater relays or data gateways. Its structural and storm-response achievement would remain independently necessary. Within the supplied roster, MNE-06 retains the specific identity of substantially improved mobile through-seawater range–rate service, including its availability and infrastructure boundaries.

change_log.change: Replaced absolute acoustic bandwidth exclusion and a strict 100 m optical cutoff with condition-dependent propagation tradeoffs.
change_log.reason: The review supports distance-dependent acoustic bandwidth and clarity-dependent optical range, including secondary reporting of a 200 m optical sea trial.

change_log.change: Narrowed the radio propagation statement to a few metres at about 10 kHz.
change_log.reason: That specific example is supported by the supplied review. The broader metres-to-tens-of-metres generalization lacks equivalent retained support.

change_log.change: Reframed the acoustic ceiling as an empirical benchmark requiring context and added the 20 kbps over 13.5 km result.
change_log.reason: The reported 270 km·kb/s example prevents treating 100 km·kb/s as a universal limit and exposes overlap with the proposed minimum rate.

change_log.change: Preserved the survey’s attributed quantitative detail with explicit access qualifications.
change_log.reason: The Fewell report has no retained text. Its envelopes and historical comparison remain unresolved rather than disproved.

change_log.change: Reframed significance around expanding existing underwater command and telemetry.
change_log.reason: The supplied review documents existing acoustic robot control, sensor collection and vehicle coordination.

change_log.change: Integrated physical bitrate, effective Ethernet bandwidth, directionality and sampled endurance for the Zhang deployment.
change_log.reason: The full-paper review materially qualifies the abstract’s account of the 30 m deep-sea result.

change_log.change: Separated Zhang’s projected optical ranges from demonstrated distance.
change_log.reason: The longer distances derive from water-sample estimates with different geometric-loss assumptions.

change_log.change: Added folded-path geometry and offline processing to the Dong result and qualified its publication metadata.
change_log.reason: These details define the demonstrated scope. The retained manuscript and failed journal access leave the supplied submission date, journal DOI and pagination incompletely verified.

change_log.change: Removed comprehensive claims about progress through November 2026.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness record is empty and cannot establish the complete contemporary frontier.

change_log.change: Clarified the proposed completion test, measurement requirements and relationship to the historical 1 Mbps benchmark.
change_log.reason: Relay topology, net rates and useful 50 km service need definitions. A stronger 10 km bitrate alone does not establish the separate operational requirements.

change_log.change: Added reproducibility boundaries and explained relationships across the full supplied roster.
change_log.reason: The final record needs testable scope and distinct concept identities. Roster-only implications are explicitly labeled synthesis.

unresolved_issues: The Fewell survey’s numerical envelopes, measurement definitions and approximately 2.5-fold historical improvement remain unverified because its text was not retained.
The complete mobile through-seawater performance frontier through 1 November 2026 remains unestablished by the supplied freshness record.
Minimum net rates at 10 km and 50 km, permitted relay infrastructure, acceptable availability, latency, power use and environmental conditions remain to be specified for the proposed demonstration.
A comparable baseline is needed to quantify the proposed improvement while accounting for mobility, deployment conditions, endurance and infrastructure.
Dong’s supplied submission date and journal DOI remain unverified within the retained manuscript, and journal pagination remains unavailable following the reported failed access.
The original source and exact wording of the historical repeater-free 1 Mbps over 10 km benchmark are not independently documented in the supplied evidence.
Related-concept explanations use the supplied roster titles. Detailed technical requirements for those other entries were not provided.
